extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, and law students concerned with U.S. patent litigation jurisdiction
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards determining when a dispute involving patents is a case arising under the Patent Laws (thus within exclusive federal jurisdiction) versus when it is a state-law contract/tort matter. Explains which facts/pleadings (validity, title, infringement, monopoly) must be in issue to import federal jurisdiction and gives examples and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence/continuance of the monopoly must be put in issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence or continuance of the monopoly must be put in issue, and submitted to the judgment of the court for permanent and conclusive settlement between the parties; mere collateral questions as to patentability, scope, or title that serve only as evidence do not make the cause one arising under the Patent Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that a controversy which is collateral and only enters the adjudication as evidence (not as an essential element of the judgment) is not a cause arising under the Patent Laws. Examples: subordinate controversies (title in actions quare clausum, truth of publication in slander) are not patent causes. See §858 and accompanying discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal jurisdiction when validity, title, or infringement are put in pleadings and enter judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal courts obtain jurisdiction on the ground of the subject-matter only when validity, title, or infringement are put in issue by the pleadings and must enter into the judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant's proofs require the court to examine conflicting patents or priority claims to determine the plaintiff's property right, the bill must be dismissed in state court because such matters are exclusively federal. (Cites Hovey v. Rubber Tip Pencil Co., Campbell v. James, Puetz v. Bransford, etc.) See §857 and §862.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action to repeal (cancel) a patent is a case affecting the monopoly (federal jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action to repeal a patent is instituted for the purpose of destroying the monopoly, puts in issue the right of the government to grant or of the patentee to receive the patent, and if successful permanently deprives the patentee of exclusive rights; such actions are pre-eminently cases arising under the Patent Laws and are within exclusive federal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes repeal actions as efforts of sovereign power to frustrate the creative act and return the invention to unpatented condition. See §859 and citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action to annul an interfering patent (between adverse patentees) is a federal case affecting monopoly
rubrics_metrics.description: An action to annul an interfering patent seeks cancellation of a rival's letters-patent and addresses the title to the patentee's monopoly; it is thus a case arising under the Patent Laws and within exclusive federal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires at least two patents covering the same invention granted to different patentees; the proceeding denies the legal existence of rival monopolies and seeks cancellation. See §860 and cited cases (Rice v. Gamhart, Satterthwait v. Marshall, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Action for infringement is a case affecting the monopoly (federal jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action for infringement directly involves the existence or scope of the monopoly or the title to the patent because an allegation of infringement asserts the invention is the proper subject of a monopoly conferred on the patentee and that the monopoly embraces the invention practiced by the alleged infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A denial of infringement necessarily controverts patentability, title, or scope and thus puts those federal issues in issue. Federal courts have exclusive jurisdiction over infringement actions, including suits by licensees and certain suits between licensors and licensees. See §861 and many cited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal courts' exclusive jurisdiction over patent validity/title/infringement extends even when collateral state-law issues are present
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclusive jurisdiction of the Federal courts over cases involving existence, validity, or infringement of a patent is not defeated by the presence of other collateral matters (contracts, trusts, fraud) that would otherwise be outside the Patent Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a co-owner who fraudulently obtains reissue and then employs infringing articles gives rise to a federal infringement action despite contract/trust breaches; licensor-licensee disputes that raise infringement issues are federal. Where monopoly is put in issue, federal jurisdiction 'draws after it' power to decide necessary collateral matters. See §862 and examples (Duke v. Graham, Stanley Rule & Level Co. v. Bailey, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts cannot assume jurisdiction over cases affecting the monopoly, even by parties' consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Where jurisdiction is exclusively conferred on one tribunal on the ground of subject-matter, no other tribunal can obtain cognizance of it; neither convenience nor consent of the parties can bestow a power that the law has withheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus, if a case truly puts existence or continuance of the monopoly in issue, a state court must dismiss or provide for removal to federal court. See §863.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract or tort actions concerning patented articles are generally not cases affecting the monopoly (state jurisdiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Breach of contract or torts to the patented article (breach of warranty, fraud, royalties, purchase-money claims, etc.) are wrongs at common law and ordinarily are to be redressed in state tribunals and do not, by themselves, form cases arising under the Patent Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The existence and scope of the monopoly are determined by Patent Law and are not altered by private contracts; such contract/tort actions remain state matters unless diversity of citizenship confers federal jurisdiction or the patent's validity/title/infringement is actually put in issue. See §864, §869.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts may inquire collaterally into patent validity when required to decide underlying state-law claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a state court cannot entertain a direct suit to repeal a patent, it may, in a state-law action (e.g., suit on a note, claim for purchase-money), collaterally inquire into the validity of the patent where that inquiry is necessary to decide the state-law issue (for instance, failure of consideration if the patent was void).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: defending a note given for purchase of a patent by proving the patent invalid; Cross v. Huntley and Bich v. Atwater illustrate admissibility of patent-invalidity evidence in state contract suits. Such collateral findings do not make the state judgment a declarative, binding adjudication of the monopoly for all purposes. See §869 and associated discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suits to cancel or enforce a license are generally not within federal jurisdiction unless diversity exists
rubrics_metrics.description: A suit to cancel or enforce a license is not within the jurisdiction of the Federal courts unless the parties are citizens of different States and that fact is alleged; otherwise such license-contract suits are state matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts have no jurisdiction over mere license-contract enforcement or rescission where parties are same-state citizens, though federal courts may decide whether a license exists if diversity supports jurisdiction. See §865 and cited cases (Merserole v. Union Paper Collar Co., Dale Tile Mfg. Co. v. Hyatt, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: When federal jurisdiction is properly founded (e.g., infringement) the federal court may grant complete relief and decide ancillary matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Once jurisdiction is acquired by the federal court on grounds like infringement, the court may grant complete relief and settle all other matters necessary to full determination, even if those other matters are not original grounds for federal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Bloomer v. Gilpin, Brooks v. Stovey. Illustrates that federal courts resolve related contract or equitable questions when necessary to fully adjudicate the patent issue. See accompanying discussion in §862 and §865.

rubrics_metrics.name: A controversy is a 'case' under Patent Laws only when issues to be settled are essential elements of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: For a controversy to be a case affecting the monopoly, the affirmations and denials must result in issues which are to be conclusively and permanently settled by judgment; controversies that are merely subordinate or collateral and supply only evidence to another cause are not 'cases' under the Patent Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the distinction between essential issues (which create federal jurisdiction) and collateral issues (which do not bind other litigation). See §858 and discussion of collateral controversies (e.g., title inquiries in non-patent suits).

rubrics_metrics.name: A co-owner cannot, in a State court, sue for compensation for use as an infringement action
rubrics_metrics.description: One co-owner of a patent cannot sue for compensation for its use by an infringer in a state court because such an action (infringement) falls under the Patent Laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example cases: De Witt v. Elmira Nobles Mfg. Co.; explains this is an infringement cause and thus federal. See §861 and related notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches or estoppel do not waive lack of federal jurisdiction over subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's laches or estoppel cannot avail an objection to want of jurisdiction; jurisdictional defects on subject-matter cannot be waived by parties' conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Creamer v. Bowers and other authorities stating that procedural defenses cannot confer jurisdiction where subject-matter is exclusively federal. See §863 and §868 notes.
